title: Why doesn't the FDA regulate herbal supplements?
summary: Josh and Chuck discuss why the FDA does not regulate herbal supplements the way it regulates drugs. They recount the herbal-uppers story of Josh's father, then argue that Americans underestimate herb potency compared with cultures that have long used them. Examples include ephedra (mahuang), which was linked to about 16,000 reported cases of death and injury between the early 1990s and 2003, angel's trumpet, monkshood, and the 1607 Jamestown militia's hallucinogenic jimsonweed episode. They explain the rise of herbs and traditional Chinese medicine, the 2003 survey finding that 70% of herb users don't tell their doctors, and the complementary and alternative medicine (CAM) movement. The core of the episode is the Dietary Supplement Health and Education Act of 1994 (DSHEA), which classes herbs as dietary supplements, shifts the burden of proof to the FDA, and limits marketing claims (for example, "quiets an anxious mind" instead of "treats anxiety"). They contrast this with the roughly eight and a half years and millions of dollars needed for drug approval, where only about 0.1% of tested compounds win approval. They also note the FDA's removal of a Chinese product containing human placenta in April 2007.
topics: Dietary Supplement Health and Education Act

segments.title: Opening banter and herbal Elvis story
segments.summary: Josh opens with a joke about the show's location and shares the story of his father's habit of taking herbal uppers and downers in the late 1990s, which he quit. He uses it to say herbs can pack a punch.

segments.title: Mahuang (ephedra) and reported harms
segments.summary: The hosts describe mahuang, known in the US as ephedra or ephedrine, and say the Chinese used the shrub for about five thousand years. After it reached the US in the 1990s, about 16,000 cases of death and injury were reported to the federal government between the early 1990s and 2003. They attribute this to American recreational abuse and a lack of respect for herbs.

segments.title: Herb potency and cultural attitudes
segments.summary: The hosts argue that Americans treat herbs as natural and harmless because they are unregulated, unlike drugs such as codeine-containing Tylenol, which is kept behind the pharmacy counter. They give examples of potent plants: angel's trumpet, which causes delirium if eaten, and monkshood, which is highly toxic to handle. They also recount the Jamestown Colony militia that ate a hallucinogenic plant and tripped for days.
topics: perception of regulated versus unregulated drugs

segments.title: Rise of herbs, traditional Chinese medicine, and CAM
segments.summary: Herbal use and traditional Chinese medicine grew in the 1990s and 2000s. A 2003 survey found that 70 percent of herb users do not tell their doctors, partly because doctors know little about herbs and may stop them. This led to the complementary and alternative medicine (CAM) movement, which the hosts describe as combining traditional and Western medicine. They explain that traditional medicine suits chronic conditions and Western medicine suits acute ones, but doctors' liability concerns kept CAM from taking off.

segments.title: Dietary Supplement Health and Education Act and FDA approval
segments.summary: The hosts explain that herbs fall under the Dietary Supplement Health and Education Act, passed in 1994, which places them outside FDA drug jurisdiction. They contrast this with drug approval, which requires animal and human trials costing millions and taking about eight and a half years, with only about 0.1 percent of tested compounds approved. Under the act, the FDA must prove a supplement is harmful before it can be pulled from shelves, and it is often understaffed and underfunded.
topics: Dietary Supplement Health and Education Act

segments.title: Marketing claims and banned products
segments.summary: Supplement makers cannot claim their products treat, cure, or mitigate disease. For example, a passion flower product can say it quiets an anxious mind but not that it treats anxiety. The hosts compare this to 19th-century patent tonic ads. They also note the FDA removed a Chinese product containing human placenta from the US market in April 2007.

segments.title: Sign-off
segments.summary: Josh and Chuck point listeners to the HowStuffWorks search bar and the podcast email address for more information and suggestions.
